items.title: What to expect from Apple's October 13 'Welcome home' releases
items.content_html:
Apple is releasing more hardware on October 13, with big expectations surrounding its smart home lineup. Beyond the HomeView, here's what you can anticipate Apple will unveil, and what it probably won't.

For product launches, Apple is best known for its September special event, which is the venue for new iPhone models like the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. However, it often holds more events in the fall than just one.

Regularly, it holds a second event in October or November, used to launch products that it didn't feel it could reveal alongside the iPhones. That is exactly the case for fall 2026.

Apple has confirmed that it will be holding a second fall event on October 13, 2026. Titled "Welcome home," it is heavily implied by Apple to be an event all about the smart home.

Again, it will likely be a prerecorded presentation recorded at Apple Park, streamed on YouTube, the Apple TV app, and the Apple Event page. Some press will be in attendance in New York City.

This will be the second set of releases under the tenure of CEO John Ternus.

As usual, AppleInsider will be reporting in-depth about the product launches.

Apple launched a lot during its September 9 "Surprise and Shine" event, including the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, and the fifth-generation AirPods.

That still leaves a lot of products waiting in the wings for an introduction. Based on rumors and expectations over the past few months, what follows is what you could expect Apple to bring out.

However, while the list includes quite a few products, the fact that the event is titled "Welcome Home" strongly hints that it will be dominated by smart home hardware.

There's also the prospect of another event after this one. The rumored October 27 event is thought to be the usual Mac and iPad event.

It's entirely possible that the rumor is wrong and Apple will bring everything out in one event. But, it seems more plausible for Apple to break the launches up in this way.

HomeView - Absolutely

Rounding out the smart home category, there is the often-rumored Home Hub. Or, at least, that's what we were referring it as pre-launch.

An October 11 report says it's actually called the "HomeView."

Intended to be the center of a smart home setup, the Home Hub may take the form of half a HomePod with a display attached. A second version is one that could attach to a wall, possibly using a magnetic stand.

A mock-up of what the Home Hub could look like.

Effectively, it will be a smart display that shows a user's notifications, calendars, and other important daily details they need to know about. It will also handle tasks like FaceTime calls, using a built-in camera.

It's a big-screen device, but it won't be a big app-using device. There will be limited apps installed, and no access to an App Store at all.

While a whole-home device, it will still maintain privacy in some way, such as checking for nearby iPhones or using AI. This should help it display information intended for a specific user, not to all home occupants.

The interface will apparently borrow ideas from the Apple Watch, including a home screen with "faces" and a "face gallery." This sounds like users will be able to set complications on the display that will be in view when not in active use.

Though it will be touch-enabled, the main way people will be persuaded to interact with it is by voice, specifically Siri. Touch will be an option, but it's not going to be essential.

It will also act as a central hub for your smart home, controlling Apple Home devices and being a central port of call for the network itself. Which is handy, considering the massive number of accessories allegedly on the way.

Security cameras and thermostats - Likely

The most recent rumors regarding the event and Apple's plans include news of an unusual partnership with LG. The partnership will see Apple co-designed but LG-branded devices including a smart deadbolt lock, indoor and outdoor security cameras, and a floodlight camera.

Despite this, Apple is said to still be working on its own range of smart home cameras. These are now expected to be launched in 2027.

Apple has also been working with Schneider to produce devices including smart thermostats, a humidity sensor, and more.

These are all new devices, but Apple is also expected to update its more familiar ranges such as Apple TV and HomePods.

HomePod mini - Absolutely

Starting off with the more probable launches, the HomePod mini is widely expected to get a refresh. Indeed, Apple's own code referenced new colors for the refreshed range.

The new models will retain the Blue, Black, and White colorways of the first-generation set, but Yellow and Orange are set to go. Instead, they will be replaced by Powder Pink and Forest Green.

An approximation of two new HomePod mini colors.

It won't just be a change in color, as it will almost certainly get a spec-bump update in the form of new chips. For the most part, the chip change to the S10 will bring with it support for Siri AI, as well as some other features.

Other code leaks have referenced a new surround sound mode in a four-speaker setup. A "Party Mode" has also been mentioned, though not exactly what that means.

Apple TV 4K - Absolutely

Continuing the smart home theme, the Apple TV 4K is also expected to get a similar glow-up to the HomePod mini. Again, the main thrust of the change will be to introduce support for Siri AI, as one June code leak indicated.

The current expectations are an upgrade to the A19 or A19 Pro chip, as well as a possible upgrade of memory to 8GB or 12GB. The chip changes will also include the N1 networking chip, one of Apple's own design.

An Apple TV 4K and Siri Remote

While the design of the Apple TV 4K itself isn't expected to change this time around, there may be a new Siri Remote. Though product identifiers say a new controller is on the way, rumors are light on what will change.

There was one late rumor on October 11, claiming that the Apple TV 4K could get a new processor in the form of the A19. At the same time, it may also gain a microphone so it can be used to talk to Siri without a HomePod or the Siri Remote.

Other than that, our best hope is for some form of ultra-wideband or Find My integration for the Siri Remote.

iPad mini - Later in October

While it was a strong contender for launch alongside the iPhones, the iPad mini is still expected to get some form of update in 2026.

This is one of those models destined for launch in late October.

The eighth-generation device's main change is anticipated to be the display. An 8.4-inch LTPS panel with hybrid OLED should bring it in line with the iPad Pro range, if not to the same standard of specifications.

iPad mini on an arm

Beyond the display, you can also count on a chip upgrade. The current favorite is the A20, along with the possible inclusion of Apple's networking and modem chips.

Smaller changes that have been rumored include a repositioning of the FaceTime camera, as well as a new vibration-based speaker to help improve water resistance.

M6 MacBook Pro and iMac - Later in October

A post-iPhone event is usually when Apple introduces new Mac products. However, following the surprise launches of the M6 Mac mini and updated Mac Studio in late August means there's fewer models for Apple to choose from.

The most obvious ones that have been rumored about are the M6 models. Catching up to the Mac mini, there are M6 models of MacBook Pro and iMac allegedly on the horizon.

The current 24-inch iMac.

The M6 MacBook Pro rumors say that it will still use a mini LED screen with ProMotion, the same six-speaker sound system, the same ports, and the same chassis as the current generation.

However, it will instead get an upgrade to the M6 chip, making it a typical Apple spec-bump upgrade.

It's a similar story for the M6 24-inch iMac, with it also thought to be given a speed boost, but retain the current design. An overhaul with OLED is expected for the iMac, but that will be far into the future.

If these are going to appear, that'll be under the late October Mac and iPad event.

OLED MacBook Pro - Later in October

One of the big-hitter rumors for the MacBook Pro line has been the display. An OLED-equipped model has been rumored about for quite some time, and observers believe it could surface this time around.

While speculation put the launch in early 2027, it's now thought to take place in October. Or at least to be announced in October with a release in November.

With the sooner event being smart home-centric, this will appear in the later October event for Macs and iPads, if it does actually turn up.

An OLED display can offer richer black tones and a higher quality image for users, while also using less power. As a touchscreen, it will also be the first MacBook to be touch-enabled, and join a notebook market that already has many touch-enabled displays.

Other than the display, you can probably expect it to be a spec-bump update, including using Apple's newer chips. But there may be a change in construction that helps it lose weight.

On October 4, a report claimed there will be a significant weight reduction, thanks to Apple redesigning components to be smaller and lighter. Whether the weight loss will be enough to get closer to the lighter MacBook Air remains to be seen.

Apple's product catalog is a lot longer than what's here, even taking into account the items that could surface in the later-October event. Instead, you can expect them to turn up in early 2027 in some form.

items.title: Apple smart home control center is called 'HomeView'
items.content_html:
Apple's new smart home controller is the HomeView, and while it's not shipping in October, you'll be able to get your hands on it before the end of 2026.

Over the last few months, rumors have intensified about a new smart home device Apple has been working on. With the October 13 event on the way and focused on smart home hardware, it's finally going to become a reality.

Posted on Sunday in Bloomberg's "Power On" newsletter, Mark Gurman writes that the smart home hub will be called the HomeView. Using a display and an A18 chip, it will work as the command center for an Apple-based smart home.

The "View" part of the name is apparently reflecting how it is meant to be a display for users, with the intention of it primarily being a voice-controlled device. The display, however, will still have touch support.

There will be little reason to touch the display either, as it's apparently not intended to be used with a lot of apps at all. It will work with a "limited selection" of Apple applications, Gurman says, but will lack an App Store and the ability to add more software.

Really, it is intended to be the nerve center for the smart home, with Siri being the main conduit for controlling it and attached devices.

The HomeView will ship in two variants. One will be a countertop model with a metal speaker base, sold in a choice of space gray, silver, starlight, and pink colorways.

The second version will be a wall-mounted edition with a flat, square base that resides just below the display while on the wall. The wall-mounted option will ship in just two colors: space gray and silver.

Currently, the HomeView is expected to ship in the middle of November. That means it will be available to consumers a month after its launch.

items.title: Where Apple focused engineering so the iPhone Duo could have desktop-like performance
items.content_html:
To make the iPhone Duo as thin as it is, Apple needed to make a lot of design choices to fend off heat. Here's what they did, how they did it, and where in the device the innovations live.

Folding devices like the iPhone Duo often raise engineering challenges due to their unique design. However, solving problems like making as thin a smartphone as possible can lead to the creation of others, such as keeping it cool.

In an interview with PCMag, Apple's VP of silicon engineering Dan Murray and senior manager of thermal product design Banafsheh Barabadi discussed how Apple fixed heat issues in the iPhone Duo.

The discussion first covered the "M-Class-inspired packaging design" of the A20 Pro, referring to a change from the package-on-package (POP) process Apple previously used. Rather than a vertical stack for the system-on-chip (SOC) and the memory, Apple moved the DRAM module next to the processor.

The "M-Class" stems from the idea that a notebook like a MacBook Pro has a lot more internal space to play with than a smartphone. The memory can easily be placed separately from the processor, rather than requiring it to be stacked to save space.

The use of a wafer-level multichip module (WMCM) packaging technique helped spread out the heat instead of confining it to one place. The location also meant that the memory still had fast communications with the chip itself.

While Apple has used vapor chambers in the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, Apple redesigned the idea for the A20 Pro used in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. The chassis were also redesigned to work better with the thermal technique.

There are four pillars to heat management, with the first being direct silicon access. The shifting of the DRAM from the vertical stack helped this, since heat from the silicon has a more direct path to the vapor chamber.

"Metal over foam" is the second pillar, creating a direct thermal and mechanically compliant coupling between the vapor chamber and chip. "It took us months of development to get the material properties exactly right," the engineers explained.

The technique was first spotted during a teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, described at the time as "thermal chainmail" inside a pad.

The third is the vapor chamber, which now as three times the surface area as the previous version, along with more de-ionized water. The chamber also serves as the "central structural plane for the device," said Barabadi, with the battery and logic board mounted directly to it.

Lastly, the fourth is a new layer on the back of the foldable display to keep it sturdy. It's described as a "nanotube copper display metal plate material" that provides mechanical strength for the display.

The copper plate also has a high level of thermal conductivity, combined with a high-conductivity graphite layer. The result is that heat is spread more evenly across the display, reducing hotspots.

"When we combine these four pillars together, it meaningfully improves the thermal performance across every metric," said Barabadi.

The thermal antics aren't just limited to the main body of the iPhone Duo. The all-important hinge does its part too.

Since the iPhone Duo has two halves, connected by a hinge, the two thin halves become one much thicker device when closed. For heat management, this is a problem, because the vapor chamber in the iPhone Duo floats in the middle.

To thermally connect the two halves of the chamber, there's a flexible graphite pipe going through the hinge. This transfers heat between the two sides, balancing the temperature throughout the devices.

It also considerably increased the surface area used for heat dissipation.

To Apple, the part needed to be worked on by both the thermal and mechanical teams. All due to being a flexible material that needed to survive thousands of hinge activations throughout the iPhone Duo's lifespan.

items.title: Just about all of 'No Man's Sky' is coming to iPhone and iPad
items.content_html:
Hello Games is bringing "No Man's Sky" to iOS and iPadOS, with preorders for the mobile version starting ahead of its October 28 release date.

"No Man's Sky" is a game that has been around since August 2016, and only became available on Mac as recently as June 2023. Now, over a decade after the initial release, "No Man's Sky" is finally landing on iPhone and iPad.

The sci-fi adventure game is set in a procedurally-generated universe, filled with countless solar systems, planets, and space stations. Starting on the outer rim, players can explore unique planets, build bases, and upgrade their ships as they try to reach the center of the universe.

While it's finally traversing the software landscape to iOS and iPadOS, the release isn't a cut-down version designed for mobile users. Instead, it's the same full universe that players on other platforms already enjoy.

That includes recent updates such as COSMOS, and the 2025 Voyagers update that introduced customizable big-rig starships.

No Man's Sky on an iPad, with interface - Image Credit: Hello Games

However, there are some small concessions, in line with the Nintendo Switch version of the game, following player feedback. There wasn't multiplayer or "settlements" on Day 1, which will be the same on iOS from launch.

It also introduces a new set of touch controls to work with the mobile displays. Players can still elect to play with controllers, mouse and keyboard on an iPad, and casting to a television for big-screen gaming.

As an ambitious game, it does take a hefty amount of storage space, but not as much as you'd think. The developers say that installation is less than 5 gigabytes, despite the sheer scale of the in-game universe.

While it is a ten-year-old game, there were inklings of a move to iPhone and iPad a few years ago.

The WWDC 2022 launch of the Metal 3 API and the MetalFX framework was accompanied by discussion of how it would be used to improve the performance of "No Man's Sky" on Mac. MetalFX is used to manage upscaling, as well as drawing extra frames to improve frame rates.

In a June 2023 interview with AppleInsider for the Mac version's launch, Hello Games CEO Sean Murray talked about how Mac and iOS was something the studio always considers. The move to Metal had taken almost two years at that point, with Apple assisting one year into the effort.

Murray was enthusiastic about the App Store and its reach to new users who may not have heard of his company's games.

However, developing for Mac and iPad are very different tasks. "Suddenly you have to consider a new user interface, battery life, things like that," Murry said, adding that you have to consider how that audience "like to play their games."

At the time, he didn't directly say a mobile edition of "No Man's Sky" was on the way, but hinted at it.

Moving to Vulkan enabled Hello Games to work with Metal, and likewise the move to VR opened up the possibility of developing for the Nintendo Switch and mobile hardware. Murray ended the thought by saying he was excited to see where Metal might lead to, and that it was "just our next step in a longer journey."

The game is available to preorder from the App Store on Monday, October 12 as part of Apple's App Store Indie Games Week. The full release is on October 28, with a free-to-try element at launch.

Unlocking the full game will cost $19.99.

items.title: When Apple is shipping the rest of its 2026 hardware
items.content_html:
Apple has yet to ship a lot of stuff that's expected in 2026. From the certain date for the iPhone Duo, through the expected ones for the HomeView, and on to the probable MacBook Pro, here's when to expect stuff in stores.

Even before Apple formally announces its range of smart home devices, it has an unusual number of products expected to be released shortly. Here's what's coming plus when it is most likely to be announced and ship.

Apple added an extra date to its cycle of announcement, pre-order, and shipping, with a "Get Ready" option on October 12, 2026. But it's still the case that it is only starting on October 16 that you will be able to give Apple your money.

Apple's iPhone Duo, in action

Then on October 23, you will get your iPhone Duo. Or you will if you were fast enough and lucky enough. More than most iPhone launches, supply of the iPhone Duo is going to be extremely constrained.

It will be in stores starting on that same date, though. Maybe, depending on how many Apple made.

Reports claim that Apple's home hub, the HomeView, will ship in mid-November.

That's around a month after the announcement, so it's a shorter delay than the iPhone Duo had. It's conceivable that pre-orders will start on Friday, October 16, but Apple might want to keep that date clear for the iPhone Duo.

An example of what the HomeView could look like.

Pre-orders will surely start by at most a week before shipping, meaning it should be by early November.

It's possible that Apple's home releases will solely feature the new HomeView plus updates to the HomePod mini and the Apple TV 4K. But Apple is also preparing cameras and other devices in partnership with LG, which would benefit from being included in the launch.

The alleged Apple-LG smart home devices - Image credit: @pdfu/X

What's definitely coming at some point is Apple co-designed but LG-badged devices including a smart deadbolt lock. There will also be indoor and outdoor cameras, and a floodlight camera.

If those are announced at the October 13 event, pre-orders and shipping will not be far behind. It's anyone's guess, though, whether these devices will be immediately available, or slip into November.

That depends on whether they are ready in volume or not. And it might be useful to compare to the HomePod mini, which at least has an expected shipping date.

Apple's own smart camera isn't expected until 2027.

Unlike the HomeView and these cameras, there is already a HomePod mini on sale at Apple, but it's no longer the one you want. Instead, expect a new HomePod mini to ship on October 30.

An approximation of Apple's new pink and green HomePod mini speakers

It's most likely that pre-orders for the new HomePod mini will open on October 23. Note that at present, the Apple Store online is quoting a delivery date of between October 20 and October 27 for most current models.

Whether it will be called Apple TV 4K or will be renamed just "Apple TV" in order to further confuse people with the same name for the streaming service and the Apple apps, a new one is about to be announced.

The current Apple TV 4K.

Consequently there is again no official date, but reports say that the new Apple TV will ship on October 30. Pre-orders will presumably be on October 23.

In this case, the online Apple Store will offer some same-day delivery of the item. But in-store pickup will likely not be until November 4.

This is one of the furthest off of the expected new devices, but it's reportedly going to be announced on October 27. It should then ship by late October or at least before the end of November 2026.

Given the logistics of shipping all the other devices to stores, and making the maximum PR impact, shipping and even pre-orders are most likely to slip into November.

The current MacBook Pro.

When it comes, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro and 16-inch will feature a higher-quality OLED screen. It will also be a touchscreen, and Apple will see if there are enough fans of that in a laptop to make it a hit.

It will also reportedly be lighter than the current model. But the key selling points will be the touch-screen and the faster M6 processor.

Also rumored to be announced on October 27 is the next iPad mini. This is to have an OLED display for the first time, although it probably won't support the fast but battery-saving ProMotion of other iPads.

The current seventh-generation iPad mini sports an A17 Pro chip for Apple Intelligence. Credit: Apple

If correct, this will be the first update to the iPad mini since October 2024.

If the MacBook Pro is far off, an updated iMac is closest to a guess. By the end of October, it will have been two years since the iMac was updated.

The current 24-inch iMac

That was with the M4 processor, so there have been rumors that it will get an M5 upgrade, and perhaps the M6 like the Mac mini. If it does, it seems most likely to be announced alongside the MacBook Pro update believed to be on October 27.

This, too, would then mean it shipping some time in November.

After pre-orders and Apple's new "Get Ready" kind of pre-pre-order, eventually all of these devices will be available. It's still the case that only the base configurations will usually be available same-day, but this is when you will be able to buy without delay:

At least some of these dates will be confirmed by Apple during its forthcoming "Welcome Home" event.

items.title: There's a vibe-coded Adobe Creative Suite clone, and it's pretty good
items.content_html:
Vibe-coded alternatives to Adobe Creative Cloud apps such as Photoshop and Premiere have been released. They may help Mac users save money, but there are some nuances to the situation.

AI has been a major driver of change in the software development landscape, and it may have claimed its biggest scalp. A group of vibe coders has decided to take on Adobe by coming up with their own alternatives.

Released under the banner of ArtCraft, the releases on GitHub are referred to as "open-source, clean-room reimplementations" of well-known productivity software. Albeit software trying to be legally distinct enough from Adobe's products to avoid a lawsuit, while still being recognizable to users.

Said to be a combination of prompts to Claude Opus and developed in Rust, the initial releases include tools like Photoshop called PhotoCraft, Lightroom redone as LightCraft, and Premiere Pro as FilmCraft. Other Adobe products appearing in the repositories include Illustrator as VectorCraft, Acrobat as PDFCraft, and After Effects as EffectCraft.

They aren't stopping there. WordCraft is a take on Microsoft Word, alongside PowerPoint's DeckCraft, Excel's GridCraft, AutoCAD's CADCraft, and Avid Pro Tools' SoundCraft.

All of the cloned projects by ArtCraft are provided without any fees. Obviously, "free" Photoshop has helped the project get a lot of attention online, and they may stick around for quite a while.

That's assuming the Adobe lawyers don't try to pound them into the ground like a railroad spike.

The actual process of how the apps are being made are not fully spelled out by those behind the recreations. However, we can guess by claim of "clean-room implementations" that the apps were vibe-coded, rather than code being analyzed and copied.

While not a direct copy of Adobe's apps, it's safe to say that there has been a fair amount of inspiration taken from the interfaces.

Adobe Photoshop [left], PhotoCraft [right]

We downloaded PhotoCraft to see just how close the project got to the original. It turns out that it's very close, to the point that someone who knows Photoshop will potentially think it's a slightly different resolution to the one they're used to seeing.

Opening a blank document and pasting it in, there are obvious differences between the applications. For example, seeing colors and gradients by default isn't what I'm seeing in Photoshop, and there's no AI suggestions bar either.

But that said, there are a lot of elements that are almost identical. The left-hand tools bar, the icons on it, and the layers panel are very alike, if just tweaked enough to be a tiny bit different.

It's the uncanny valley, but for user interfaces.

We're very familiar with subscription services and the associated ire, especially when it comes to Adobe Creative Cloud's very high monthly fee.

However, the situation with what ArtCraft is doing is a difficult one to judge from a legal standpoint.

Assuming it's true, and we have no reason to to believe it isn't, the whole "clean-room" claim means that it's not a case of someone telling an AI to decompile code.

The classic example of that is Phoenix Technologies and American Megatrends making their own version of the IBM BIOS for PC clone manufacturers to use. That was found to be legal, after almost a decade of courtroom fights about it.

If the Adobe app clones were made legitimately without looking at the code, or decompiling the product being copied, then that becomes less of a legal issue.

What does remain a problem is recreating the overall interface. While there are typical conventions in play when it comes to user interfaces for specific kinds of apps, there is usually some level of variance between them.

Sure, you can rearrange the GIMP interface to be more like Photoshop's UI, but even that isn't directly copying every single element. The original GIMP layout is also a very different animal.

Here, copying the interface design is on purpose.

GridCraft [left], and VectorCraft [right]

The problem becomes one of finding where the line in the sand is. That, and working out what Adobe's well-funded legal team will be tempted to fight over.

As usual for a legal fight involving a major company, Adobe doesn't even have to win, but instead threaten others with expensive litigious action. That alone is a hefty threat.

While this may feel like a legal issue that can affect end users, it's tough to work out what could ultimately happen to them.

This isn't direct piracy of a product. You're not downloading Photoshop illegally, but someone's vibe-coded version of it.

But at the same time, since it is software that has been produced quickly using AI, it may not necessarily have the same style of battle-hardened code as the real thing. Indeed, the current iterations aren't at feature parity with the real things right now, and may never get there either.

The code is open-source though, and we know people are poring over it as we speak. From a security standpoint, so far, we haven't seen any untowards internet traffic to strange servers while using the apps.

What this does demonstrate is that anyone with enough money to pay for lots of Claude or ChatGPT tokens can quickly come up with full applications. Some that can look and act like apps made by a major corporation.

While this may seem like a potential lawsuit-based train wreck in the making, the next big attempt to take on Adobe could go a different route. One that stands up on its own, without leaning on Adobe's interface and feature set as a template.

That's what Adobe should be worried about.

items.title: New HomePod mini and Apple TV will debut during HomeView launch
items.content_html:
While the HomeView home hub will be the headline device, Apple's "Welcome Home" event will finally debut the new Apple TV set-top box, and a refreshed HomePod mini.

On October 13, 2026 Apple is expected to launch a major push into the smart home market with what's to be called the HomeView. Now Bloomberg claims that, as expected, there will be new versions of the HomePod mini and Apple TV.

Specifically, the report backs up previous rumors regarding the HomePod mini refresh. It says that this will come in a new series of colors, and feature an S10 processor for faster performance.

Those colors have previously been reported to include powder pink and forest green for the first time. Previous colors blue, black, and white, will also be available.

Then a new update to the languishing Apple TV 4K will see it get a new processor. However, it is said to be the not-Pro version of the A19 rather than the expected A20 Pro.

This new Apple TV will reportedly also come with microphones so that users can talk to Siri without a HomePod or the Siri Remote. Then a revised Siri remote is said to come with a speaker to help with finding it.

The new HomePod mini and Apple TV are due to be in stores and shipping on October 30.

items.title: Tim Cook visits China for the third time in 2026
items.content_html:
Apple executive chair Tim Cook has returned to China for the third time in 2026 alone, greasing the political wheels and insisting Apple wants to do more in the country.

While he is no longer CEO, Tim Cook's new role as executive chair allows him to speak on behalf of the company on a political level. While John Ternus settles into his CEO chair, Cook is continuing to glad-hand to help Apple grow.

According to the South China Morning Post on Sunday, Tim Cook has made his third visit to China for 2026. He was spotted in a few places, including taking time to talk to the governor of Guangdong, Meng Fanli.

Guangdong is home to a large number of Apple's suppliers and partners in the country, with the region known for being a manufacturing center.

Cook told Meng that Apple was willing to expand its presence in the region, including improvements in smart manufacturing and growing its sales channels.

In response, Meng said the provincial government welcomed Apple's increased presence, and that it wanted to forge a "first-class business environment."

Cook's visit wasn't just to meet Meng. He was also spotted at an Apple Store in Guangzhou, and watched a local content creator film a martial arts video with an iPhone 18 Pro.

"Great to be back in China!," Cook wrote to his Weibo account on Saturday.

The visit marks Cook's third trip to China in 2026, and his first as Apple's executive chair.

His first was in March, visiting Apple stores in Chengdu and Beijing to mark Apple's 50th anniversary. He also spoke at the China Development Forum.

The second was in May, forming part of a U.S. technology and business delegation following U.S. President Donald Trump to a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

items.title: Updated entry-level iPad won't arrive until early 2027
items.content_html:
While there will probably be a launch of the OLED iPad mini in late October, users face a long wait until early 2027 before they get to see a revised base-model iPad.

Apple is poised to hold a pair of events in October, with the smart home-centric one confirmed for October 13. A second is apparently planned for October 27 for new Macs and the OLED iPad mini, but it may be a little light on other iPad models.

In Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman writes that the later Mac and iPad event should be the last Apple launches of the year. That means a bunch of expected products will be bumped into early 2027 instead.

That list includes things like updates to the MacBook Air and MacBook Neo lines, the second-generation iPhone Air, and the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e. For iPads, the list includes the iPad Air and iPad Pro refreshes, and the entry-level iPad.

The claim is in line with Gurman's previous reporting in July, which also outlined an iPad mini update in October followed by Q1 2027 for the iPad. Again, iPad Air and iPad Pro updates were scheduled for the spring.

As for what to expect from the next entry-level iPad, code leaks in September pointed to the use of an A19 chip and 8GB of memory, making it capable of running Apple Intelligence. The model is also thought to have a C1X modem with sub-6GHz 5G support, as well as Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread thanks to the N1 networking chip.

Pricing is currently expected to be the same as the current model, starting at $449.

items.title: ADT rumored to handle installations in Apple's smart home push
items.content_html:
Apple's smart home plans could involve yet another partner, with security company ADT potentially joining the roster alongside LG and Schneider Electric.

Since early October, the rumor mill has been rife with claims that Apple will be using companies like LG and Schneider to help its smart home revival effort. However, job listings indicate that there could be a third company that will lend a hand to Apple.

Job listings for ADT have appeared across the United States since July, calling out for a "Low Voltage Technician," reports MacRumors. While some have been hired for the positions, it seems they haven't been given much information about their actual responsibilities.

Some successful applicants have disclosed since then that they have been shadowing other existing ADT technicians, as they waited for more information. Employees and managers have also signed non-disclosure agreements for the role, heightening the secrecy level as per usual for Apple.

A second clue is that these hires were provided with iPhones. Other ADT technicians work with Android devices, implying the selected workers have a need to use Apple's ecosystem.

Hires have also mentioned that ADT plans to hand out more information about the roles later in October. It is plausible that ADT is waiting for Apple's announcement to take place before doing so, meaning it could happen on October 13.

As for what ADT could provide to Apple customers, it seems that it won't be about ADT-produced hardware, and more assisting consumers with installations. Managers have told the new hires that it was to do with home automation and installation services.

At face value, this sounds like Apple providing an option for ADT to install new smart home devices for consumers. At least, the trickier devices that require some level of DIY skills to mount on a wall.

Candidates for these include LG's plethora of security cameras and a wall-mounted thermostat, as well as Apple's wall-mounted version of the HomeView. Schneider has also been linked to the effort, which brings in more thermostats to the picture.

While ADT does offer its own home security hardware and monitoring services, the rumor doesn't seem to indicate anything about new Apple-specific hardware.

It remains to be seen if ADT will be providing more than technician services for Apple.

items.title: The Magic Mouse is 17 years old, it's time Apple fixed it
items.content_html:
The Magic Mouse will be 17 years old on October 20, 2026. It's beyond time Apple turned it from a curiosity into something that Mac owners actually want to use.

Apple officially unveiled the original Magic Mouse on October 20, 2009. It would ship with all iMacs, but existing Mac owners could buy one for $69.

At the time, Apple made a big thing about it being "the world's first multi-touch mouse," and it was right to. Remember, this was just two years after the iPhone introduced multi-touch to the world.

Ditching the buttons that were familiar to all computer users, the Magic Mouse had a single surface for users to tap. Tapping the left side initiated a left-click, with the right side becoming a right-click.

But the lack of buttons is what made the multi-touch possible. Gestures across the surface allowed Magic Mouse users to scroll content, swipe through timelines, and pan and zoom images.

This all sounds great, as it did 17 years ago. But there were problems and, with a refreshed model six years later, Apple's use of a belly-up charging setup made matters worse. Years later, Apple still hasn't addressed most of the issues putting people off buying a Magic Mouse.

Now, as the Magic Mouse hurtles towards yet another birthday, it's time that changed.

It's fair to say that for as futuristic and distinctly Apple as the Magic Mouse was, it was never universally liked. There was no native middle-click support, and gestures for some staple Mac OS X features were missing.

Other issues actually made the mouse unusable for some. Reports of Bluetooth instability affected some Macs more than others. Even if the mouse stayed connected, its low-profile design was uncomfortable for a lot of people.

This was perhaps the biggest drawback, and one that made the Magic Mouse an ergonomic nightmare. And this all happened a year before Apple design chief Jony Ive's form-over-function approach at least partially caused the iPhone 4's antennagate issue.

The Magic Mouse also used standard AA batteries. Apple even began selling its own rechargeable batteries and a charger to go with them.

It took Apple six years to add a built-in rechargeable battery.

Six years later, on October 13, 2015, the Magic Mouse 2 was announced alongside the Magic Trackpad 2. For the first time, a Space Gray option joined the standard White model, although it was initially only bundled with the iMac Pro. Yet more colors came with the M1 iMac refresh in 2021.

Apple made two main changes to the Magic Mouse 2, neither of which were well received.

Apple still hasn't moved its port

The addition of a rechargeable battery was initially welcomed. But Apple's decision to place the Lightning port on the bottom of the mouse is still mocked online to this day.

Apart from looking ridiculous, the port placement had a very real impact on usability. Being unable to use the mouse while charging it was a huge drawback, and one no other wireless mouse suffered from.

Apple also chose not to bring Force Touch from the Magic Trackpad 2 to the mouse. This was a problem for some who found that, because the whole surface of the mouse moved when clicking, it trapped their palm when it did.

The Magic Mouse 2 went unchanged until 2024, when Apple removed the Lightning port. Adding a USB-C port could have given Apple the chance to move it to a more traditional position, but it didn't.

So, here we are. We're uncomfortably close to the Magic Mouse's 17th birthday. It's basically the same mouse that went on sale in 2009, warts and all.

Apple could refresh the Magic Mouse at any moment, and I have to imagine that it will at some point. When it does, there are a few easy wins that I'd love to see Apple jump at.

The Magic Mouse is just uncomfortable to use

The most obvious fix would be to move the USB-C port to the edge of the mouse that cables normally protrude from. This is a solved problem, and every other mouse maker in the land knows it. It's time Apple got on board.

Apple may argue that a five-minute charge gives users enough juice to get through a full day of use. But that's an excuse for poor design, not a reason for it to remain that way.

I'd also like to see physical left and right buttons make a return to Apple's mouse. They're more ergonomic and add a tactility that the current whole-mouse-click situation doesn't afford.

That might mean Apple ditching the gestures that have made the Magic Mouse so magic to date, but not necessarily. The Logitech MX Master 4, for example, lets you press a button, then perform a gesture by moving the mouse itself.

Another quick win would be to remember that people use these things for more than five minutes at a time. The low-slung, smooth-like-a-dolphin approach looks great, but it makes for terrible ergonomics.

I'm genuinely curious whether anyone at Apple uses the Magic Mouse for any length of time each day. I doubt it. There's a reason every other mouse is shaped higher where it's gripped and lower at the buttons.

Unfortunately, all of these changes require the Magic Mouse to be completely redesigned. And that's probably why they won't happen.

But they absolutely should. And until they do, the Magic Mouse will always be a novelty that most iMac buyers throw in a drawer, never to see the light of day again.

items.title: Dumb down your Mac: Save 12GB by removing Apple Intelligence
items.content_html:
Mac users who don't want Apple Intelligence to take up precious drive space can free up capacity thanks to a new command-line tool.

Apple Intelligence is generally a good set of features for Apple's ecosystem of devices. However, not everyone particularly wants to use it.

That is especially a problem for Mac users with small drives and constrained spare capacity. For those stuck with a 256GB SSD, recovering 12GB can be extremely useful.

While the answer for this particular segment of Mac users would be to uninstall or remove Apple Intelligence, it's not that simple.

You can turn off Siri, but you can't delete the Apple Intelligence models in the macOS Settings at all.

Under macOS 27, there's no option to turn off Apple Intelligence at all. You can turn off Siri, but there's no single point in the menu to disable Apple Intelligence completely.

Even if you manage to disable Apple Intelligence, there's still data hanging around and no direct option to remove it. There are about 12 gigabytes of models that Apple Intelligence relies on, and that's storage users could find other uses for, if they were allowed to delete it.

Without a single Apple-sanctioned option to remove AI in the Settings, Mac users will have to look elsewhere for a solution.

A project by Om Lahore called RemoveMacAI aims to clean up your Mac of Apple Intelligence. It's a free project, released on GitHub under the MIT license.

RemoveMacAI is a script that installs a configuration profile to disable Apple Intelligence features on a Mac. That includes features like Siri AI, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, and more.

The start of running RemoveMacAI on a Mac mini.

As well as disabling features, it also removes the Apple Intelligence foundation models, as well as those for image generation, Spatial Photos, Photos Clean Up, and Xcode code completion.

The script's configuration profile works on restriction keys for Apple Intelligence, as well as for settings that don't have a restriction key. The models are removed using Apple's asset service, with System Integrity Protection enabled and System files kept intact.

Once deleted, the profile also redirects attempts to download each removed model to a closed local port. This prevents macOS from redownloading the models again.

However, you can remove the configuration profile to restore previous settings and allow the models to redownload.

AppleInsider recommends that users check out the project and ensure they are aware of what RemoveMacAI does before running it.

While there are a few ways to run RemoveMacAI, the easiest is from a single line, pasted into Terminal. At the time of publication, that line is:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omlahore/RemoveMacAI/main/install.sh | bash

Ran in Terminal, it downloads RemoveMacAI to a temporary folder and automatically runs. It shows how many features are active, how much storage space the models consume, and warns you about what happens if you proceed further.

At the prompt to "Turn Apple Intelligence off? [Y/N]" type Y, then enter.

A Device Management pop-up will appear, asking if you want to install the configuration profile. Click Install, and the script will continue to delete the models.

To revert the process, use this similar line in Terminal:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omlahore/RemoveMacAI/main/install.sh | bash -s revert

items.title: iPhone Duo will greet some owners by name on its first boot
items.content_html:
New owners of the iPhone Duo will get an extra treat if they buy it from an Apple Store, with the option to personalize the smartphone's boot-up screen to greet them by name.

The iPhone Duo will be available to the public from October 23, with preorders starting from October 12. However, for some customers who opt for the full in-store Apple purchase experience, they can get an extra bit of personalization.

According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman in an X post late on Friday, Apple's retail stores will have a system that will modify the boot process of the iPhone Duo. When booted up, the iPhone Duo will show on screen "Hello" followed by the owner's name, such as "Hello, John" when it turns on for the first time.

While it isn't clear how this is done, it may lean on Presto, Apple's system for updating the software of in-stock iPhones that are still stored in their unopened packaging.

Stores will have a system to make the change, Gurman adds. However, there is no mention of whether this can be adjusted or disabled after purchase.

Not every customer will be able to benefit from this level of personalization. It will apparently only be available in U.S. Apple outlets, for the iPhone Duo, and only in English or Spanish.

items.title: My Apple TV 4K is now 'vintage,' and I'm ready for a new one
items.content_html:
My 2017 Apple TV 4K is so old that it's now considered to be a vintage product, but that's fine, because there's a new model on the horizon with some features that I can't wait to try out.

Apple routinely adds products to its vintage list when it last sold them more than five years ago, but less than seven years ago. It means that those products might be harder to get parts for, should a repair be needed.

As of October 9, 2026, the 2017 Apple TV 4K has been added to that list. I already knew that this thing was showing its age, and that it was probably time for an upgrade.

But years of lackluster Apple TV hardware updates left me waiting for something new and exciting. On the hardware front, that never really happened, but with the 4th-gen Apple TV 4K rumored to be days away, I can't wait to see what Apple has been cooking up.

To be very honest, the rumors have so far pointed to the new model looking very much like the old one. And it'll, of course, run tvOS, like all other Apple TV 4K generations.

But as the not-so-proud owner of an Apple TV that's almost a decade old, there are some key features I'm keen to try out. The new model can't come soon enough for me.

I think it would be a good idea to remind everyone just what the original Apple TV 4K had to offer. At the time, it was pretty great, but it's severely limited in 2026.

The first thing I want to call out is the Siri Remote that my family and I have been subjected to for so long. The 1st-gen Apple TV 4K came with a glass Siri Remote. The one with a huge touch surface at the top.

It sucked in 2017, and it sucks in 2026. There's a reason Apple ditched it with the 2nd-gen Apple TV 4K.

On a more positive note, the Apple TV 4K was the first Apple TV to support 4K video. The name might have given that away.

On the inside, the whole thing was powered by an A10X Fusion chip straight out of the iPad Pros of the time. 32GB and 64GB models were offered.

Connectivity-wise, HDMI 2.0a included support for 4K with Dolby Vision and HDR10. A Gigabit Ethernet port was a welcome sight for those of us running home media servers, too. Dual-band 802.11ac WiFi was offered for those not willing to run cables everywhere.

In short, the Apple TV 4K was a product of its time. But that time is long gone.

With the stage set, it should be clear why I'm keen to upgrade. There are a few reasons, if we're going to be specific about things.

The Siri Remote

I think there's a world where I'd seriously consider upgrading to a new Apple TV 4K generation just to get a new Siri Remote. Yes, I know I could just buy one of the newer models and use it with my old box, but I can't bring myself to spend that kind of money when the old one still kinda sorta works.

The new Apple TV 4K can't come soon enough

Sure, our current Siri Remote is cracked, and every time I try to seek through a movie, I want to hurl it at the TV, but still. $59 for a new remote was never going to happen until this one got lost or embedded into a screen somewhere.

I look forward to clicky buttons. I look forward to instantly knowing which way up the remote is without having to look at it even more.

But as annoying as the Siri Remote is, it's far from the only reason I'm ready for a new Apple TV 4K.

Raiders of the Lost eARC

Our Apple TV 4K is hooked up to a pair of HomePod minis, which makes for a pretty great audio experience. Watching movies and TV shows sounds impossibly better than using the TV's small, tinny speakers.

But I don't just watch movies and TV shows. Look behind our TV, and you'll find an Xbox Series X and a PS5. Look beside it, and there's a Nintendo Switch 2 and a Steam Deck.

But playing games on any of these things means using those crappy TV speakers or resorting to headphones. I enjoy using headphones for late-night gaming sessions as much as the next guy, but I don't want to use them exclusively.

That's where HDMI ARC, or eARC, comes in. Already supported by every Apple TV 4K except my 1st-gen unit, eARC is nothing short of magical.

The TL;DR of it all is this: eARC can send audio from any device that's connected to a compatible TV to the Apple TV 4K instead. And thus, to whatever they use as their audio output.

In my case, that's those HomePod minis. And I cannot wait to play Cyberpunk 2077 on my PlayStation through those.

Playing games locally

Every so often, Apple reminds everyone that the Apple TV 4K can play games downloaded from the App Store. And it's right, but the 1st-gen Apple TV 4K's A10X Fusion chip just isn't up to the task and hasn't been since the COVID lockdown.

The 4th-gen Apple TV 4K is upon us

If the rumors are accurate, the 4th-gen model will use at least an A19-class chip. And that's a huge upgrade.

Whether that's an A19 or A19 Pro remains to be seen, but if I had to put money on it, I'd go with the latter, just given economies of scale.

The more premium chip just makes sense when we remember that the new Apple TV 4K will support Siri AI. An A19 Pro will give it plenty of vital headroom, considering these things don't get updated very often.

We've already seen what the A19 Pro can do in terms of gaming, and the prospect of an Apple TV 4K with one beating at its heart could be a boon for Apple Arcade and beyond.

Four-HomePod surround sound

Recent rumors suggest Apple will add support for using four HomePods with an Apple TV 4K in some kind of surround sound setup. As someone already using two HomePod minis, this intrigues me.

There are plenty of questions, though. We don't know if this feature will be limited to the new Apple TV 4K, although I doubt it will come to the 1st-gen model regardless. After all, it doesn't even support tvOS 27.

We also don't know which HomePods will work with this rumored feature. Not only is it unclear whether it will require full-fat HomePods or just HomePod minis, but we don't know if it will require new smart speakers.

We'll find out soon enough, but for now, the idea is enough to whet my appetite.

By now, it should be clear why the 4th-gen Apple TV 4K has my attention. Upgrading from one generation of Apple TV 4K to another is rarely warranted. But after nine years, it's time.

If everything goes the way we expect it to, Apple will announce the 4th-gen Apple TV 4K on October 13, 2026. It'll be joined by Apple's other "Welcome Home" products, including a new HomePod mini (possibly just new colors) and the oft-rumored Apple home hub device.

The countdown is on. My Siri Remote is on notice. And maybe, finally, my TV will feel safe once more.

items.title: Right on schedule, sources claim iPhone 18 Pro orders have been cut
items.content_html:
There's a reason we've built some contacts in China, and refuting supply chain sources saying that demand for the iPhone 18 Pro is so low that Apple has cut back production is one of them.

In October 2025, it was that the iPhone Air orders might be be changing. In 2024, the iPhone 16 was definitely doomed. Or in 2022, it was that Apple might have have scaled back orders for the iPhone 14.

Now Nikkei Asia is reporting that suppliers have been told to cut component production because of low demand for the iPhone 18 Pro. Specifically, one of its sources said Apple has been more conservative with its component orders since early September.

That seems questionable. Although the iPhone 18 Pro was announced on September 9, 2026, pre-orders didn't start until September 12. But then another source says no, it was in August that Apple either cut orders or placed lower ones than usual.

AppleInsider did note that pre-order shipping dates were taking longer to slip back than in 2025, but also that there are reasons for that. Apple never says how many components it has ordered, or how many iPhones it made for launch.

Plus in 2026 it has three "Pro" grade iPhone launches including the iPhone Duo, and it has split its iPhone launches with the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e maybe coming in the spring.

"We do find the demand in terms of volume from August for the second half of this year is not as strong as previous years when all the new models are introduced all together," one source in the supply chain cited by the report obviously said. "This year, the standard iPhone 18, which could provide a boost to volumes, will not require components until toward the end of the year, for launch in early next year 2027."

"Could" is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that quote. An iPhone line, launched six months after the last one, will provide a boost to volumes.

There is also the fact that of the premium models launched, the iPhone Duo is the most high-profile one, especially for the September and October buying crowd. And Apple is not shipping that until more than six weeks after announcement, meaning production started later too.

So Apple has launched fewer iPhone models and isn't placing component orders for the next releases just yet. That does not account for Apple later scaling back component production, but it does entirely account for orders overall being lower.

What does account for these reports of scaling back orders is that Apple calibrates how many parts it needs to have on hand like this every year, sometimes even several times a year. It then gets dutifully, possibly even gleefully, reported as the iPhone being in trouble.

When the same claim comes every single year, you have to question whether these sources have the whole picture. More often than not, there's some kind of bonus paid to writers that move the stock market, like Forbes does.

As is typical for Nikkei Asia, it really has no idea what to do with information it gets from the supply chain. The report only gives lip-service to the iPhone Duo and the split-launch as factors in why, maybe, Apple may have a different amount of Pro orders than it had a year ago.

And, we know from our sources that today, whole-unit assembly orders for the iPhone 18 Pro have not been cut. That says more about the claims than anything else.

items.title: At just 5.2mm, Apple's iPhone Air 2 might miss the point
items.content_html:
Assuming a new rumor that the iPhone Air 2 will be even thinner than the current model is true, Apple is focusing on the wrong thing and might push buyers even further away from its ultra-thin and light smartphone.

At 5.6mm thick, the iPhone Air is the thinnest iPhone Apple has ever made. Even a year post-launch, it still feels like it could be snapped in half just by picking it up wrong.

It could be argued that the iPhone Duo will take the thinness crown, albeit only when opened, after its October 23 launch. It'll come in at just 5.2mm thick when unfurled, but with a chunkier 11.3mm measurement when closed.

It's easy to see how Apple could go thin with the iPhone Duo. After all, it'll have a much larger footprint to fill with chips and battery than a normal iPhone.

But now it's been claimed that the iPhone Air 2 will also slim down to the Duo's 5.2mm thickness. It'll essentially be an iPhone Duo snapped straight down the middle.

But while the same rumor claims the iPhone Air 2 will come equipped with iPhone 18 Pro battery tech for increased capacity, I find myself concerned.

If the iPhone Air feels impossibly thin already, the need for it to get even thinner seems dubious at best.

At worst, it could be enough to stop iPhone Air 2 buyers in their tracks.

It's surely fair to say that, as fond as I am of the iPhone Air, I'm in the minority. It's equally fair to say that it hasn't been a big seller for Apple, but it also hasn't been the sales catastrophe mostly unnamed sources from China said it was.

I've heard various reasons why people have chosen to ignore the iPhone Air to date. But there are two that keep cropping up: battery life and the camera situation.

I wasn't convinced that either was a real issue when the iPhone Air launched in 2025. I even took it on vacation to find out for myself and, spoiler, it was fine.

The thinnest iPhone yet, for now

But there's no denying that, alongside an iPhone 17 Pro, the iPhone Air had its limitations. The battery life was worse, and it had two fewer cameras. Stats are stats.

It didn't help that the iPhone Air was priced like an iPhone 17 Pro, either. I would imagine it was a very difficult sell for Apple Store employees the world over.

For me, the trade-offs were worth it. I loved how thin and light the iPhone Air was, and I still do. More so after writing our iPhone 18 Pro Max review.

But for most people, the choice was easy. "I'll have the phone that lasts longer and takes better photos, please."

The question was always going to be whether the iPhone Air 2 would address those issues.

We've been hearing for some time now that the iPhone Air 2 will feature a battery with a larger capacity than its predecessor. That should equate to an ability to go longer between charges.

If the rumors are true, Apple will achieve that by using denser battery technology than that previously used. Boiled down to one sentence, the new tech allows more power to be stored in a battery of the same size.

But there's a catch. Again, if the report is accurate, the iPhone Air 2 will be even thinner than before, reducing the amount of space inside it.

That would, presumably, mean the iPhone Air 2's battery will be physically smaller than the one used in the iPhone Air. And that should be fine, because the capacity will still be higher than before.

Except, it's all a missed opportunity.

The iPhone Air has been great, but some still have concerns

The theory makes sense, at least. Apple seems to have chosen to make the iPhone Air 2 even thinner because it can use the higher-density battery technology to balance things out.

But, given that potential buyers complained about battery life the first time around, I'm not sure this is the right approach. Instead, it would have made sense to keep the thickness the same, use the new battery tech, and post even better battery life figures.

This approach would wipe out the battery life complaint for good. It just wouldn't be an issue.

Apple is well aware of what pushed people away from the iPhone Air. Rumors claim the Air 2 will gain another camera, after all.

There's just no reason not to truly fix the battery issue once and for all. Especially for the sake of 0.4mm.

I'm using an iPhone 18 Pro Max that I reviewed right as my main driver now, so I fished my iPhone Air out of a drawer when I saw the new rumor that its successor would be even thinner. I'm not sure what benefit there is to a phone being even thinner than this.

After doing some research, it seems that there have been thinner phones. Although many of them are foldables, and the figure only applies when they're open, just like the iPhone Duo.

For standard phones, the thinness crown seems to go to the Vivo X5 Max. Launched in 2014, it measured just 4.75mm and somehow still found room for a headphone jack.

The Oppo R5 also launched in 2014, measuring 4.85mm. Oppo couldn't make the headphone jack fit, though.

Next, there's the Micromax Canvas Sliver 5. It had no camera bump whatsoever, yet still measured just 5.1 mm. It launched in 2015.

2016 saw Motorola try its hand at the thin phone thing. The result was the Moto Z, measuring an iPhone Air 2-like 5.19mm.

After that, it's basically foldable phones (when open) and then the iPhone Air in 2025. We aren't talking about tablets, but if we were, the 13-inch iPad Pro sits at 5.1mm.

The fact that all of the world's thinnest glass slab phones are from a decade ago is telling. Companies tried it, but ultimately went back to thicker devices afterwards.

Even Samsung's thinnest-ever phone, the Galaxy S25 Edge, is thicker than an iPhone Air. At 5.8mm, it's nowhere near the thinnest phones ever made.

Maybe this should tell us something. Maybe going even thinner is a fool's errand; once you reach around the 5.6mm mark, it's thin enough.

I'd suggest that is very much the case. And I bet anyone wishing for significant battery and camera gains for the iPhone Air 2 would agree.

items.title: Redesign your new M6 Mac mini for 2026 with these colorful wraps
items.content_html:
Apple's M6 Mac mini still comes only in silver, making vinyl skins an easy way to give the compact desktop a more personal look. Our favorites add style without bulk while helping protect the aluminum finish from everyday scratches and fingerprints.

A vinyl skin makes the most sense for anyone who wants to change the Mac mini's appearance while preserving its compact footprint. Unlike a case, a skin provides cosmetic protection rather than meaningful protection against drops.

The 2026 Mac mini keeps the same dimensions as the enclosure Apple introduced with the M4 generation, measuring 5 inches square and 2 inches tall. The shared dimensions keep many M4-era skin designs relevant to the newer Mac mini.

XtremeSkins already sells a product specifically labeled for the M6 Mac mini, while Slickwraps, ArmorSuit, and Capes continue to list their skins for the 2024 model. The biggest differences come down to design, material, coverage, and price.

Slickwraps has one of the more colorful Mac mini collections, including a Retro Series built around old-school computer and gaming-inspired designs.

The $32.95 Retro Series comes in matte or gloss finishes and uses precision-cut vinyl rather than a generic sheet that buyers have to trim themselves. Slickwraps says the material helps protect against scratches, scuffs, and fingerprints, and can be removed without leaving adhesive behind.

There are nine Retro Series designs, along with separate collections built around solid colors, carbon fiber, marble, wood, metal, camouflage, and other finishes. Slickwraps also lets buyers upload their own artwork for a custom skin.

Slickwraps still labels its current Mac mini collection for the M4, which shares the same exterior dimensions and basic port arrangement as the M6 model.

Unused and unapplied non-custom skins can be returned within 14 days of delivery. Slickwraps also offers one replacement under its Goof Policy if a customer botches the installation, though shipping and handling still apply.

XtremeSkins already has a collection specifically designed for the M6 Mac mini. The company sells separate pieces for the top, bottom, sides, and Apple logo.

Buyers can use one finish across the machine or mix different materials and colors.

Options include matte colors, carbon fiber, brushed metal, wood, concrete, camouflage, textured finishes, and printed designs. Prices currently run from about $8 to $21, depending on the pieces selected.

XtremeSkins says its skins use air-release adhesive and can be repositioned during the initial installation. The company says it designs and manufactures the skins in Britain using templates made specifically for the M6 enclosure.

The vinyl can help prevent fingerprints, scratches, and scuffs without adding the bulk of a case.

ArmorSuit sells a two-pack of Mac mini vinyl wraps for $35.77, with dozens of finishes ranging from carbon fiber and brushed metal to bright matte colors and textured designs.

ArmorSuit says its products are made in the United States and backs the Mac mini skin with a 30-day money-back guarantee. The company was founded in Southern California in 2010.

The current product is still labeled for the 2024 Mac mini, which shares the same exterior dimensions as the M6 model.

MightySkins sells Mac mini skins specifically listed for the M6 alongside the M4, M4 Pro, and M5 Pro models.

The $19.99 Two-Tone Hex design comes in matte, carbon fiber, or glossy glitter finishes. MightySkins says it uses 3M vinyl with air-release technology for easier installation and adds a laminate layer for protection against scratches and everyday wear.

The company says its skins are precision cut and can be removed without leaving adhesive residue. MightySkins has operated as an American-owned company since 2008.

Finishes include transparent matte, carbon fiber, leather, solid colors, and several graphic designs. Capes says its skins are cut for individual devices and can be removed without leaving adhesive behind.

The current Capes product page is still labeled for the 2024 M4 Mac mini, which uses the same 5-inch-square enclosure as the M6.

Lefxmophy has a 4.8-star rating from 10 reviews and also comes with Amazon's 30-day return policy. The seller lists the sleeve specifically for the 2024 M4 and M4 Pro Mac mini.

Vinyl skins remain the better choice for changing the Mac mini's appearance without adding much material. Silicone cases trade some of that slim profile for more coverage around the aluminum enclosure.

None of these accessories turns the Mac mini into a rugged computer. Their main job is to protect the finish and make Apple's little silver box look more personal.

items.title: If we trust it, Home Hub privacy could lead a smart home revolution
items.content_html:
A new Apple Home hub could kill "smart" appliances, but only if Apple can succeed in convincing us its devices don't retain audio and video recordings.

There is a rumor of an Apple-made accessory that resembles a large tube of chapstick that could accompany Apple's rumored Home hub tablet. It would have a sensor in it that captures footage at a low frame rate, but doesn't actually "record" video.

I discussed this on the AppleInsider Podcast as an interesting concept. Instead of needing a computer chip in every component of our home, Apple could use such sensors to "understand" statuses around the home.

Forget having a smart dishwasher that needs a Wi-Fi connection. Instead, have a sensor see that you've started a dishwasher cycle.

In the Home app, you could see "dishwasher running" as a status in the Kitchen. The same goes for the washer, dryer, or other appliances.

Apple already has systems in place for this thanks to the AI analysis features of Apple HomeKit Secure Video. As models improve, I could see an Apple TV running basic sensor analysis locally to provide these system statuses.

The video summaries are brief, but understandable. "Someone arrived home and unloaded groceries" is possible today, so it isn't a stretch to think these tools could provide statuses for your home and appliances.

Imagine you're loading the dishwasher, but your home is aware someone else is in the shower across the house. Siri could alert you and suggest waiting until the person exits the shower, perhaps even setting a reminder for you.

I think the future of the smart home is a more intelligent, more proactive system that doesn't need everything to be smart. In this case, AI analysis of environments, that are local and private of course, could enable so much more than a simple Wi-Fi-connected appliance.

Apple has spent more than a decade convincing us it is the go-to for privacy and secuity

The problem will be convincing people that these devices aren't cameras and aren't recording video. My shower example would need some kind of smart water valve or shower component, or if you trust it enough, one of these sensors in the bathroom.

The level of trust users would need for such a device is immense. Apple wants to sell us on an Apple Watch that "listens" without recording audio, so it will need to sell us on a camera that doesn't record video too.

If you can't trust one of these in the bathroom, then Apple has failed.

I understand that the bathroom and living room are two very different places. If you can't trust the sensor to be totally private in one where you're changing clothes, you can't trust it in the living room with your children either.

I understand some people reading this are startled at the concept. I wanted to highlight a very specific scenario that intrudes on our privacy the most.

I think Apple could attempt to pursue a truly "smart" home by taking a step back and doing more with what people already have. Apple is uniquely positioned to pull something like this off thanks to its commitment to privacy.

AirTag is a perfect example. It's a device literally capable of tracking a person, and after some concerns were addressed via software, they became the go-to for tracking.

We're totally fine with AirTags in spite of their potential for abuse

I'd much rather buy one of these little Apple sensors or hub tablets than a whole new washing machine or shower system. Plus, when the inevitable new appliance comes out or software updates stop, I'm left with an expensive brick.

If you're in a rental home, then replacing appliances and other objects with smart devices isn't an option either. Sensors that provide home status alerts that show up in Apple Home would be huge boon to people in that situation.

Again, it's going to require a lot of trust. If Apple is developing this technology, this is how I'd see it implemented, otherwise I'm not sure why they'd bother.

I'm aware this is all wish-casting and speculation, but I wanted to provide a brief idea of what I'm thinking about here. This is an answer to "what could Apple even improve about the smart home?" before the event on October 13.

Whatever the case, we'll see what Apple announces on Tuesday and see if it is moving towards a better smart home. Not a home built around making people dumber and lazier, but one that's able to act and react to the user's needs privately, intelligently, and usefully.

That is what I want from my smart home. Let's see what Apple delivers.
