items.title: Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone review: Awkwardly packaged real optical zoom
items.content_html:
When you add shutter buttons and lenses to an iPhone, it should improve the experience. The Telesin Master Grip Kit takes usable photos, but doesn't improve the experience or output, and is too expensive.

I love iPhone photography and Apple has done a lot of work to ensure its computational photography system provides the best and most personal output with each photo. Sometimes, adding accessories can help enhance the experience and elevate the end product, but that isn't always the case.

I've been testing the Telesin Mater Grip Kit for iPhone for a few weeks and I've struggled to find a reason to implement them in my photography workflow. Unlike other iPhone camera lens kits I've tested, like those from ShiftCam or Sandmarc, Telesin's is awkward to use and comes with some weird caveats.

Get 15% off with promo code DCDSOGAX at Telesin.

I didn't have the best experience, but the lenses get the job done when the right conditions are met. The resulting photos are optically better than just using your iPhone and "zooming" beyond 100mm, but require special hardware and an app.

There are two lenses for sale that appear to be only available with a pre-configured kit. You don't need both, but Telesin doesn't give you the option of buying both if you wanted to.

Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone review: attach a lens for more optical zoom

Either lens can be attached to the Main or Telephoto camera on the iPhone using the Master Grip Kit case. Telesin suggests that the 3.5x is only meant for the Telephoto camera on iPhone, but the ReefColor app supports both cameras fine.

The case has a removable plate for the lens attachment. It's useful for if you want to keep the case on but don't intend to use the lenses at that time.

The lenses thread in with a standard size, so you can use the Telesin lenses with more advanced cases like one from Tilta Khronos. Telesin's case is a good quality material with plenty of grip and isn't bulky.

The MagSafe Grip has a mode dial, zoom lever, function button, and shutter button. It houses a 3,200 mAh battery that charges your iPhone via MagSafe while attached.

Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone review: 3.5x coupled with 40x zoom gets you to 1,000mm

The base of the Grip has a USB-C port for charging, a power button for turning on the charging function, a wrist strap hole, and a 1/4" threaded hole for tripod mounting. I am not a fan of this grip for several reasons.

First, the lanyard provides a false sense of security. If you drop your iPhone while using the lanyard, the Grip will be spared, but the MagSafe connection won't always keep the iPhone attached, and may send it flying into the ground.

Do not rely on the lanyard or MagSafe connection in this way. You'll break the lenses or iPhone very easily the one time the MagSafe doesn't hold.

Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone review: these controls are virtually useless versus real camera controls

The Grip is also overly complex with all of these controls that only work in the ReefColor app. The Mode Dial swaps filters, which is pointless, while the zoom lever controls the artificial crop of the sensor.

Telesin would have been better off offering a simple shutter button and calling it a day. I ended up using the on-screen controls for everything anyway.

The remainder of this review will focus on the lenses themselves. The Master Grip is a poor add-on that other companies like ShiftCam have done much better in the past.

Whichever lens you pick, you'll need the ReefColor app to use them. That's true even if you choose to ditch the Master Grip itself.

Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone review: better optics at 2x or 3.5x

The reason being due to the lenses requiring an incredible crop of the sensor to work. When viewed through the iPhone Camera app, you see a tunnel and circle cutout where the lens obscures your view.

Now, there is some AI upscaling magic and filters helping the output of the ReefColor app. The result is a decent photo in most conditions that actually benefits from the optical characteristics of the lenses.

Sadly, needing a separate app and a crop of the sensor to achieve these photos renders these lenses almost pointless. What's worse is these kits are sold at a higher price than the premium lens options from companies like Sandmarc.

Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone review: ReefColor takes a significant crop to account for the lens

Sandmarc's lenses don't need a special app and don't unnecessarily create a circular cutout of your sensor. Telesin's optics might provide a good output, but the tradeoffs and third-party app make it much less desirable.

The 2x and 3.5x multipliers will tell you what limits you can shoot at with each lens. The 2x defaults to 105mm on the Main camera while it defaults to 200mm on the Telephoto.

That tells me that the 24mm Main camera needs a 2.2x crop before it can use the teleconverter lens. It's a worse 2.8x sensor crop to achieve the Main camera's 240mm with the 3.5x teleconverter lens, which might be why Telesin is hesitant to recommend using it that way.

The 3.5x teleconverter still needs a slight crop on the Telephoto camera to achieve a default 400mm zoom. It goes up to 1,000mm in the app, which is the same as maxing out to 40x in the Camera app.

Again, the results are usable, and the optic advantage of these lenses are visible in the output. I'm not sure how much can be attributed to the app's AI enhancements, cropping, and stabilization features.

There's also a built in stabilization feature that tries to utilize the space on the sensor not being used for photo capture. The problem is that it can feel drifty in use.

When taking some of these photos, I noticed that centering the subject in the frame took some patience. I would move the camera to center the object only to have stabilization fight me.

The feature can be turned off if needed.

Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone review: the 2x lens is more versatile while the 3.5x lens needs a lot of distance from the subject

The 2x on the Main camera is good for getting optically more pleasing photos versus Apple's 2x optical-like sensor crop.

Note that there is a minimum focus distance problem, especially with the 3.5x lens. You'll need to be around 16 feet away from the subject when using the 2x or 26 feet away when using the 3.5x on the Telephoto camera.

At the end of the day, the best camera is the one you have on you, and you have to wonder how often you'll be adding these lenses to your iPhone before taking the shot. These are also both magnifying lenses for getting closer to a subject, so they're not as multi-purpose as a wide-angle.

Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone review: external lenses can help, but iPhone takes amazing photos on its own too

I've enjoyed these kinds of camera lenses that bring a new level of optical quality and magnification to the iPhone that isn't otherwise possible. Telesin's fall short of being quite as good an experience.

These lenses work, and the Master Grip itself is fine, but at this price, I can't help but say to go elsewhere. ShiftCam is more expensive, sure, and you won't get a MagSafe grip when paying similar prices for lens and case combos from Sandmarc, but your experience will be much better.

If those other brands don't meet your needs or fit your budget, then you're better off just using the lenses already present on your iPhone than buying Telesin's.

If you buy this photography kit and use it as advertised, you will get decent quality photos. That said, my issues with the incredible sensor crop and lens design persist, and I'm not sure how to address that.

The lenses work, but requiring an app to ensure the sensor is cropped enough to prevent the lens from being in frame is odd. It's not something other premium iPhone lenses encounter, nor do you need other apps to use them.

Other camera lenses are better.

The Telesin Master Grip Kit for iPhone sells for $229.99 direct from Telesin, but exclusive promo code DCDSOGAX knocks 15% off, bringing the cost down to $195.50.

You can also pick up the Master Grip Kit at Amazon, although the retailer is selling it for full MSRP.

Customers can download popular apps such as YouTube, Netflix, Gmail, and Google Docs directly from Google's store. They won't need the workarounds previously required to install those apps on Fire tablets.

The Alexa Tablet 8 is the smallest and cheapest model at $229.99. Its 8.7-inch display sits inside an aluminum body weighing just 329 grams, making the tablet small enough for comfortable one-handed reading.

Amazon includes an eight-core processor, 4GB of RAM, 64GB of storage, and Wi-Fi 6 support. The company promises up to 14 hours of video playback, and a 128GB configuration is available for $279.99. Buyers can choose from Graphite, Rosette, and Teal.

The Alexa Tablet 11 starts at $329.99 with 64GB of storage, while the linked 128GB configuration costs $379.99. Both versions include 8GB of RAM, an eight-core processor, and an 11-inch 2.5K display with a 90Hz refresh rate.

Dual speakers with Dolby Atmos support handle audio, while Amazon rates battery life at up to 15 hours of video playback. The tablet also supports an optional $59.99 pen and a $79.99 keyboard case, with Graphite, Amethyst, and Matcha color options.

At the top of the lineup, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts at $499.99 with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. It features a 12-inch 2.8K display with a 120Hz refresh rate and a 3:2 aspect ratio, giving users additional vertical space for documents and multitasking.

The larger tablet also includes a 4nm eight-core processor, Wi-Fi 6E, and four speakers supporting Dolby Atmos. Amazon claims up to 16 hours of video playback.

There's also a Nanomatte version with anti-glare glass developed alongside Corning. The entry-level Nanomatte configuration starts at $549.99 with 8GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, while the linked 16GB RAM and 256GB model costs $679.99.

The Nanomatte display uses precision-etched glass to reduce reflections while preserving image detail. It's intended to make the screen easier to see in bright surroundings without relying on a conventional matte coating.

For anyone planning to use the 12 Pro for work, Amazon offers a $149.99 magnetic Pro Keyboard and an $89.99 Pro Pen. The keyboard includes a trackpad, while the stylus supports 4,096 pressure levels, tilt detection, and wireless charging.

The entry-level Tablet 8 and Tablet 11 configurations include sponsored lock-screen advertisements. Amazon also offers versions without the advertisements for an additional charge.

The Alexa Tablet 8 is closest in size to Apple's iPad mini, which starts at $599. Apple's 8.3-inch tablet uses the A17 Pro chip and supports Apple Pencil Pro, while Amazon's slightly larger 8.7-inch alternative costs $369 less.

Amazon's 11-inch model competes more directly with the standard iPad, which starts at $449. The Alexa Tablet 11 costs $119 less in its base configuration and offers a 90Hz display, compared with the iPad's 60Hz screen.

Apple's tablet uses the A16 chip and includes 128GB of storage at its starting price, twice the capacity of Amazon's cheapest 11-inch model.

Despite its Pro branding, the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is a closer comparison to the 13-inch iPad Air than the iPad Pro. Apple's M4-powered iPad Air starts at $949, compared with $499.99 for Amazon's regular 12 Pro.

Amazon offers a 120Hz display at the lower price, while Apple's iPad Air uses a 60Hz panel. The iPad Air also supports Apple Pencil Pro and Magic Keyboard, with access to Apple's iPadOS software and device ecosystem.

All three tablets include Alexa+, allowing customers to ask questions, control smart home devices, and interact with Amazon's assistant without leaving their current apps. Users can summon Alexa by voice or through an on-screen button.

An optional On-Screen Intelligence feature lets Alexa examine what's displayed and respond to questions about it. For example, customers can ask the assistant to compare products they're browsing or add dates from a displayed schedule to their calendar.

Amazon says screen access is disabled by default and must be enabled by the user. A visual indicator also appears whenever Alexa can see the display.

The tablets come with a free Alexa+ experience, so buyers don't need a Prime membership just to use the assistant on their new devices. A Prime membership or separate Alexa+ subscription is required for full access to Alexa+ across compatible Alexa and Echo devices.

Readers also get a dedicated Kindle mode that silences notifications, reduces blue light, and offers three display themes. Amazon claims battery life can reach 20 hours while reading.

All three Alexa tablets begin shipping October 14 in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Shipping to the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain begins October 19.

items.title: Leaker doubles down on new iPad mini not having ProMotion
items.content_html:
A leaker with an average track record insists that the next iPad mini will have a 60Hz display, meaning it can't have the variable refresh rate that makes the device seem faster while helping battery life.

While rumors of an OLED iPad mini have been around since at least December 2024, most reports have predicted a launch by the end of 2026. A great many of those reports, though, have come from the same leaker, who is now also repeating their earlier claims about its display.

"Regarding the refresh rate of the Apple iPad mini OLED," leaker yeux1122 writes on Weibo. "There have been some mentions of 120Hz from overseas sources... however, it has already been confirmed that the domestic production units use LTPS."

By saying it will use LTPS, the leaker is stressing that the iPad mini will not have the LTPO technology needed for a variable refresh rate. "It is 60Hz — period," they conclude.

This 60Hz is the speed at which the screen refreshes, and it's significant because it's a fixed speed. The OLED displays on the iPad Pro can vary between 10Hz and 120Hz, which means they can speed up when needed.

So if you're watching a movie or playing a game, the screen — or even just part of it — will refresh faster and feel more responsive. If you're just reading a website, the screen slows down the refresh rate to save battery life.

This is called ProMotion, and if the leaker is correct, this forthcoming iPad mini will not have it. There is the fact that because it's OLED, it will be a higher-quality screen, but it's also probable that it won't be as bright as the display on the iPad Pro.

Separately, other reports have claimed that the new iPad mini may have the A20 Pro processor, as used in the iPhone 18 Pro.

items.title: Owning an Apple Home: second-party accessories could be the reboot we need
items.content_html:
Matter was meant to take the guesswork out of the smart home, but as more accessory makers silo themselves in their own ecosystems, Apple needs to take dramatic action on Tuesday.

At first, it made sense that Apple would have some background partnership with LG to get a few new products built for Apple Home onto the market. New clues found in code made it clear that Apple has much larger ambitions that should become clear during its "Welcome Home" event on October 13.

I love Apple Home, but anyone that uses it as their primary smart home will agree that it has been caught in a rut. Smart home accessory makers have noticed too, causing some of them to start siloing themselves off into their own walled gardens.

Matter was supposed to fix all of this. Apple even offered HomeKit as the basis for Matter, yet it dropped the ball on supporting the latest version of the standard.

Now, it seems as if smart home devices are getting more complex while Apple clings to an ancient app UI, layout, and feature support. The October 13 event needs to rectify this, and second-party accessories are just the start.

When news showed up about Apple working directly with LG on Apple Home products, like thermostats and door locks, everyone was confused. Sure, Apple worked with LG in the past, but given the recent news about LG smart TVs spying on users and Apple's privacy-first stance, the timing felt odd.

Second-party accessories approved by Apple will mean better Home integrations

Once code revealed that Apple is working with multiple manufacturers dubbed "second-party" for Apple Home, it became clear. It wasn't that Apple specifically chose LG to usher in a new generation of smart home products, but it had a broader plan in the works.

The news of LG being involved appeared first because its devices were in regulatory approval. Images have even leaked alongside pairing animations.

Schneider is the second company on the list, but it is highly unlikely that these are the only two brands in play. I fully expect a screen will appear on Tuesday showing multiple brands that have pledged to participate.

Second-party means these aren't made by Apple, but they may as well have been. Apple likely created a spec requirement, think "Made for iPhone," and told companies what it expected its home products to offer.

HomeKit Secure Video is a must for any Apple Home camera

Things like HomeKit Secure Video, NFC pairing, Apple Home Key, and other Apple Home integrations are a given. When you power on one of these second-party accessories, a modal sheet similar to AirPods or Beats will slide up from the bottom of your iPhone.

It's not enough that an accessory simply connects via Matter anymore. It needs to actually fit into the Apple ecosystem as more than an on/off toggle.

I don't expect that Nanoleaf, SwitchBot, Govee, or other manufacturers like them will rush out to release products that meet Apple's second-party standards. However, the ones that do will become priority purchases for those of us that want a more integrated Apple smart home.

For me, that's enough. Sure, we're back to the XKCD "one more standard" problem, but putting an easy-to-identify label on products that work best in Apple Home makes things easier.

Govee makes an interesting light that connects over Matter, but you need the Govee app to control it

The difference between second-party devices today and "Made for HomeKit" a decade ago is things like Matter. You're no longer isolating yourself to Apple's ecosystem by building for its certification.

Something about this tells me that previous rumors about Apple building its own smart home products is just this. Internally, Apple prototyped and built various devices, like smart bulbs, cameras, and thermostats, to define this second-party spec.

However, rumor mongers suggest that Apple is in fact still on to release its own devices. We won't see those on Tuesday, but they're coming eventually, allegedly.

There will be at least three Apple Home products revealed on October 13: a new Apple TV 4K, an updated HomePod mini, and the long-rumored Apple Home Hub tablet.

It's time for a new HomePod mini

Each of these plays a role in making people care about Apple Home in the first place. They're what get you into the door, not the accessory you add to it.

The push for "artificial intelligence" in the industry has only added more confusion for buyers to wade through. Alexa's AI upgrades still don't work as expected, and Google slaps "AI" on everything even when it isn't.

Apple has an opportunity to integrate Apple Foundation Models and AI-like features into Apple Home without making things worse. Unlike its competitors, it isn't totally reliant on investors to ensure it has a future, and therefore, doesn't need to grift with false promises of an AI-driven future.

The smart home will do just fine with AI analysis of activities to enable better controls and automations. I don't need my HomePod to vibe code a website — I just need it to turn on the damn lights when I tell it to.

My colleague William Gallagher has had an embarrassingly bad time with Siri AI when dealing with Apple Music requests. It's as if the assistant dumped all of its knowledge of music in the transition from an ML to AI backend.

I expect that the agentic training for Siri AI as a music assistant has been held back for this release. That, and I am also willing to bet the improved logic for parsing smart home commands will arrive Tuesday as well.

A new Apple TV 4K will see a large leap in performance

Sure, you might need a piece of new hardware to make it happen, but if it works, it'll be worth it. When I tell a HomePod to toggle a light, it shouldn't need to send the request to a server, and more local processing could ensure that's the case.

The Apple TV 4K is a must when every smart TV has Samba technology and other logging tools sniffing out your every move. Bundling in more AI smarts, better gaming options, and a new Siri Remote is just icing on the cake.

I'm also excited at the prospect of using four HomePods as a home theater system, but that's a different story.

The rumored Home Hub tablet has been detailed plenty enough before, so let's not dwell on it too much here.

The Home Hub tablet will be smaller than iPad mini and display information passively

It's a six-inch tablet that will work closely with your existing Apple ecosystem. Apple's pitch on this device will make or break it, so let's see what it is before we talk about it further.

The point is, all three of these new product categories will get people into Apple Home. Then, second-party accessories will tell customers where to get the best smart home experience.

It's Apple's classic halo effect at work.

I'm aware that my level of commitment to Apple Home is unusual for the mass-market, but not amongst the AppleInsider reading contingent. I want to do everything in the Apple Home app, and I'm tired of needing a new app every time I test a new smart home product.

The Apple Home app needs a full redesign

I expect most regular people who have an iPhone and maybe a couple of smart bulbs and maybe a fancy coffee machine that needs an app don't care about this. They'll buy the thing, install the app, and get on with their day.

Once you get past two or three additional apps, it becomes a nuisance. Most don't get that far in their smart home setups, but the fact it can happen at all is a problem.

Apple needs to rethink Apple Home as an app just as badly as it needs to reboot the ecosystem.

Rumors haven't had anything on what Apple might do with the Apple Home app, if anything, at the October 13 event. That's likely due to Apple's absolute secrecy when it comes to software.

Here's my two cents: use existing APIs like widgets to surface third-party accessory controls not supported by the Home app. Instead of demanding accessories fit into a rigid set of categories or controls, let developers control how their accessories look and are controlled within the Home app.

It's time for new ideas in Apple Home

This could lead to some ugly mishmash situations. Apple could mitigate that with some basic requirements on maintaining consistency, but that could lead us back to square one.

I'm not here to come up with a solution, only to point out that the current system is old and broken. I'm excited for new Apple Home products and the initiatives around it, but that needs commitment from the software side as well.

So much of this stops mattering if the app experience sucks. Apple needs to fix that.

Second-party accessories will help the situation by giving users a go-to for the best Apple Home solution. However, only introducing those with no software changes would be a band-aid on an increasingly irritating problem.

Apple is only a few days away from revealing its plans, so let's hope for some good news on all fronts. New Apple hardware, second-party partnerships, and a revitalized Home app experience could transform the platform overnight.

Yet another report from yet another source that has no real idea what Apple or its suppliers are doing, conflates parts orders with iPhone production. As before, this means nothing for iPhone demand.

As AppleInsider recently pointed out, and investment firm JP Morgan even more recently agreed, Apple has not cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro. Now a new report says that it must have cut those orders, because it's raised how many of the iPhone Duo it wants built.

According to Chinese financial news site STCN, Apple has increased orders for the iPhone Duo by 30%. This is for devices expected to be sold before the end of 2026.

The report seems to presume, for one thing, that manufacturing is a zero sum game for Apple. So if the iPhone Duo is up 30%, it says that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max orders are therefore reduced by up to 15% each, which is absolutely not the case.

But it also says that the new, higher order for the iPhone Duo does not exceed 10 million units. Rather than being an exclusive as claimed, that same figure was reported back in July.

Only, even if that means this new report has backing for its iPhone Duo figures, the percentages don't work.

Say iPhone Duo is now on exactly 10 million orders, and that it was therefore previously on around 7 million. This report claims that to make three million more of the iPhone Duo, Apple has cut three million iPhone 18 Pro orders.

But separately Apple is predicted to make around 80 million iPhones across the new Pro line and the iPhone Duo, in the last calendar quarter of 2026. Since Apple never releases figures, it's impossible to know, but it's easy to guess that a 30% drop in iPhone 18 Pro orders would be more than three million units.

Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro Max.

Perhaps this is all because it's a confusing report in machine translation, but we've spoken to some more fluent folks than us, and they too think it's poorly sourced and written. It also appears to count the iPhone Duo as one of the Pro models, which is why it further calculates that the total amount of orders has not changed.

Then if the math wasn't enough, it appears that the entire report is based on components rather than finished iPhones. Apple has many manufacturing partners and uses many more component suppliers around the world.

As it has always been, component increases or decreases has very little to do with the number of iPhones produced.

So while it's possible that interest in the iPhone Duo has tempered that for the iPhone 18 Pro, none of this report is able to stand that up. And in the meantime, iPhone 18 Pro orders are such that shipping takes 10-12 days.

Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo begin on October 16. The device will ship, and be in stores, on October 23.

items.title: Beats meets Pokemon in an upcoming speaker collaboration
items.content_html:
Gotta catch'em all! Beats has teased a new collaboration with Pokemon that looks like a new co-branded Beats Pill design.

Apple subsidiary Beats by Dre is no stranger to collaborations. They've worked with designers and stars like K-pop singer Jennie to brands like Nike. However, in its latest tease, it's going to be working with a heavyweight in kids entertainment.

In a short clip posted to X, Beats proposes it's "Time to catch something new." The clip shows what seems like a Beats Pill speaker with a barely visible color scheme, bombarded by light.

The visible spark elements on the speaker grille may indicate a character like the electric-type Pikachu will be on the front.

Time to catch something new. https://t.co/Rt0IfTKENC

The mini-ad also uses cartoony flashes, flames, and electric sparks, reminiscent of the characters' abilities in the Pokemon game. The clip ends by showing the Beats and Pokemon logos.

AppleInsider reviewed the updated Beats Pill in 2024, with it scoring 4 out of 5. While it was a bit weighty, it offered excellent audio quality and battery life for $149.99.

items.title: Apple & Samsung dominate the smartphone market amid decline
items.content_html:
While global smartphone shipments fell to their lowest quarterly level since Q3 2012, Apple and Samsung both managed to capture well over a fifth of the market.

Though it remains to be seen whether the iPhone 18 Pro will be as big of a success as Apple hopes, the company is seemingly moving in the right direction In its Q3 2026 financial report, Apple revealed that iPhone revenue rose to $54.25 billion, up 21.7% from $44.58 billion in Q3 2025.

Now, a report from Counterpoint Research has put this success into perspective. It offers a good idea of how iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro shipments factored into the global smartphone market as a whole throughout Q3 2026.

Due to the ongoing industry-wide RAM shortage, worldwide smartphone shipments reportedly saw a 20% decrease year-over-year. Even so, the market was dominated by Apple and Samsung, and both companies managed to increase their market share.

According to Monday's report, iPhones accounted for 22% of all global smartphone shipments, falling only behind Samsung shipments at 23%. Though the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are priced higher than its respective predecessors, both models reportedly saw a stronger launch in China and India.

Other smartphone manufacturers, meanwhile, were seemingly not as successful. Xiaomi's market share dropped to just 10%, down from 14% in Q3 2025. Oppo and Vivo held 9% and 8% of the market, respectively, down from 12% and 9% in the preceding year.

Overall, the iPhone seems to be doing better than ever, even with the absence of the base model iPhone 18. We also have yet to see how the iPhone Duo will affect Apple's position in the global smartphone market, as the foldable iPhone won't reach consumers before October 23, 2026.
